classification.difficultyReason: Multiply each numerator and denominator by the whole-number factor needed to obtain the supplied denominator.

questions.mappingNote: Page 2 explicitly demonstrates multiplying both fraction components; pages 3–4 reinforce equivalent fractions and rewriting with common denominators. This question supplies 63, so no HCF or LCM computation is required.
questions.methodNote: Multiply numerator and denominator by the same non-zero whole number to form an equivalent fraction. Here the specified denominator determines the multiplier.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Multiply each numerator and denominator by the whole-number factor needed to obtain the supplied denominator.

classification.difficultyReason: Order three fractions by finding equivalent fractions with a common denominator.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly assesses ordering fractions with different denominators. Solutions follow Example 3 using exact equivalent fractions, rather than decimal approximations.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 explains equivalent fractions; page 3 demonstrates simplification. Page 4 explicitly teaches comparison using equivalent fractions with a common denominator, with Example 3 finding the LCM and ordering numerators.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Order three fractions by finding equivalent fractions with a common denominator.

classification.difficultyReason: Add two or three fractions with equal denominators, simplifying or converting improper results to mixed numerals.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts directly apply Example 4: a produces a whole number; b, d, e and f produce mixed numerals; c additionally simplifies the resulting fraction. Page 21 provides broader fraction-addition context but no additional method is needed here.
questions.methodNote: Page 19 states that fractions with the same denominator are added by adding their numerators, and improper results should normally be written as mixed numerals in simplest form. Example 4 on page 20 demonstrates adding two and three equal-denominator fractions and converting the result to a mixed numeral or whole number.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Add two or three fractions with equal denominators, simplifying or converting improper results to mixed numerals.

classification.difficultyReason: Find common denominators, add fractions and express improper results as simplified mixed numerals.

questions.mappingNote: All nine parts directly assess the different-denominator addition identified by the printed Example 6a cue. No supplied reuse candidate has the same complete task.
questions.methodNote: Example 6a finds the LCM, rewrites each fraction with that denominator, adds numerators, then converts an improper result to a mixed numeral. Page 5 requests simplest-form fractional parts.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find common denominators, add fractions and express improper results as simplified mixed numerals.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply equivalent fractions with a common denominator to nine direct subtraction calculations.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and i change one denominator; b, d, e, f, g and h change both; c uses denominator 231 and simplifies the result. All directly assess subtraction of fractions with different denominators.
questions.methodNote: Example 6b uses the LCM of the denominators to form equivalent fractions, then subtracts the numerators. Page 5 establishes simplest-form answers; Examples 7–9 retain this common-denominator method.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply equivalent fractions with a common denominator to nine direct subtraction calculations.

classification.difficultyReason: Subtract mixed numbers using common denominators, regrouping a whole when necessary.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts directly assess mixed-number subtraction from Example 7b, explicitly referenced beside question 6. Parts b, d and e require regrouping; parts a, c and f permit direct subtraction after conversion to equivalent fractions.
questions.methodNote: Example 6 establishes common denominators. Example 7b subtracts mixed numbers by converting fractional parts to a common denominator and regrouping one whole when needed; it also supplies a whole-part and fractional-part subtraction alternative. Example 9 demonstrates conversion to improper fractions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Subtract mixed numbers using common denominators, regrouping a whole when necessary.

questions.methodNote: Examples 6 and 7a use equivalent fractions with a common denominator, add whole and fractional parts, and regroup an improper fractional sum. Example 8 applies fraction addition to a total in context.
